note: Original, written for OpenPath (CC0). Not educator-reviewed: every question is provisional and can never verify mastery until reviewed and released.

chapter.title: Same size, different pieces
text: Two fractions are equal when they cover the same amount of the same whole. Cut the same strip into more pieces and the shaded length does not change.

chapter.title: What changes and what stays
text: Cutting every piece into 2 doubles the number of pieces (the bottom) and doubles the number of shaded pieces (the top).
chapter.tip: Multiply the top and the bottom by the same number. Adding the same number does not work: 1/2 is not 2/3.

screens.title: One strip, two cuts
text: Put a strip cut in halves above the same strip cut in eighths. Count the eighths under one half.

strategies.title: Multiply top and bottom by the same number

screens.title: Find the multiplier
text: Look at the parts you know. 3 became 12: that is × 4. Do exactly the same to the other part.

strategies.title: Use the times table you know

screens.title: It is a multiplication fact
text: Each equivalent fraction hides a multiplication: 1/4 = 3/12 because 1 × 3 = 3 and 4 × 3 = 12. If the fact is slow, say the times table first.

chapter.title: Equal parts
text: A fraction names equal parts of one whole. The bottom number says how many equal parts; the top says how many we mean.

screens.title: Check the parts are equal
text: First check that every part is the same size. Then count the parts you need.

chapter.title: Same pieces
text: When the bottom numbers are the same, the pieces are the same size. Then the fraction with more pieces is larger.

screens.title: Count the pieces
text: 3/8 and 5/8 are both made of eighths. Compare 3 eighths with 5 eighths.

chapter.title: Add the pieces, keep their size
text: 3/8 + 2/8: three eighths and two eighths make five eighths. The bottom names the piece; it does not change.

strategies.title: Count pieces of the same size

screens.title: Pieces are the unit
text: Read 3/8 as '3 eighths'. 3 eighths + 2 eighths = 5 eighths, just like 3 apples + 2 apples.

chapter.title: A fact you can rebuild
text: Every multiplication fact can be rebuilt from facts you already know: a near fact, a split, or doubling.

screens.title: One more group
text: 7 × 8 is one more 7 than 7 × 7. If you know 7 × 7 = 49, add 7.

strategies.title: Split it into facts you know

screens.title: Split the 8
text: 8 = 5 + 3. Seven fives and seven threes are facts you know. Add them.

screens.title: 8 is 2 × 2 × 2
text: Start from 7 × 2 = 14 and double three times: 28, then 56.

strategies.title: Add groups one at a time
See the groups as an array

screens.title: Rows of dots
text: Draw 8 rows of 7 dots. Count 5 rows (35) and 3 more rows (21).

chapter.title: Rows of squares
text: A 6 by 4 rectangle holds 4 rows of 6 unit squares: 6 × 4 = 24.

screens.title: Length × width
text: One row has 'length' squares; there are 'width' rows.

chapter.title: Across, then up
text: A point (x, y) is x across from the origin, then y up (negative: left or down).

strategies.title: Across first, then up or down

screens.title: Walk to the point
text: Start at (0, 0). Walk x across, then y up.

chapter.title: Area under a graph
text: ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx is the area under y = f(x) between x = a and x = b. Under a constant it is a rectangle.

screens.title: Width × height
text: Under y = c from x = a to x = b: width b − a, height c.

chapter.title: Factor pairs
text: Factors come in pairs that multiply to the number: 12 = 1 × 12 = 2 × 6 = 3 × 4.

screens.title: Pairs
text: Try 1, 2, 3, … and stop when the pairs meet.

chapter.title: Zero products
text: If a product is zero, one of its factors is zero. Factorise, then set each factor to zero.

screens.title: Multiply to c, add to b
text: For x² + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. They give the factors.

screens.title: Squares are never negative
text: x² is x × x. It is 0 or positive for every real x, so x² = −1 has no real solution and x² = 49 has two: 7 and −7.

questions.prompt: A strip is cut into 2 equal parts and 1 part is shaded. The same strip is cut into 4 equal parts instead. How many of the quarter parts cover the same shaded length?
questions.solution: 1/2 of the strip is the same length as 2/4: two quarters fit in one half.

misconceptions.says: One quarter is only half of the shaded half. Two quarters cover it.
4 quarters cover the whole strip, not just the shaded half.

questions.prompt: Fill in the box: 1/3 = □/6
questions.solution: 6 is 3 × 2, so multiply the top by 2 as well: 1 × 2 = 2. So 1/3 = 2/6.

misconceptions.says: Adding 3 to the bottom does not mean adding 3 to the top. Equal fractions come from multiplying both by the same number.
The bottom was doubled, so the top must be doubled too: 1 × 2 = 2.

questions.prompt: Fill in the box: 2/5 = 6/□
questions.solution: The top went from 2 to 6, which is × 3, so the bottom is 5 × 3 = 15.

misconceptions.says: From 2 to 6 is × 3 (not + 4). Multiply the bottom by 3 too: 15.
The idea is right (× 3), but 5 × 3 = 15.

questions.prompt: Using the strips: 1/2 = □/8
questions.solution: Cut each half into 4 equal pieces: one half becomes 4 eighths.
questions.hint: How many eighths fit in one half of the strip?

questions.solution: Each quarter is 2 eighths, so 3 quarters are 6 eighths.

misconceptions.says: Adding 4 to the bottom and to the top does not keep the fraction the same. Each quarter is 2 eighths: 3 × 2 = 6.

questions.solution: 3 × 4 = 12, so multiply the top by 4 as well: 2 × 4 = 8.
questions.hint: What do you multiply 3 by to get 12? Do the same to the top.

questions.prompt: Four times what is 12? Use it: 1/4 = 3/□
questions.hint: The top went from 1 to 3. That is × 3.

misconceptions.says: From 2 to 6 is × 3, not + 4: 7 × 3 = 21.

questions.prompt: Which fraction is equal to 2/3?

misconceptions.says: 4/5 adds 2 to the top and 2 to the bottom. That does not keep the size.

questions.prompt: A recipe needs 1/2 cup of milk. Asha's measuring cup is marked in eighths. How many eighths should she pour?

misconceptions.says: From 3 to 9 is × 3, not + 6: 2 × 3 = 6.

questions.prompt: A pizza is cut into 4 pieces of different sizes, and 1 piece is eaten. Is 1/4 of the pizza eaten?
questions.solution: Quarters must be 4 equal parts. With unequal pieces we cannot say 1/4.
options: Not necessarily: the pieces are not equal

misconceptions.says: A fraction counts equal parts. 1 of 4 unequal pieces is not 1/4.

questions.prompt: A chocolate bar has 6 equal pieces. Ravi eats 2. How many sixths are left?

misconceptions.says: 2 pieces were eaten; 4 are left.

questions.prompt: A ribbon is cut into 8 equal parts and 3 are used. How many eighths are left?
questions.hint: Count the equal parts that are not used.

questions.prompt: A cake has 10 equal slices. 7 are eaten. How many tenths are left?
A garden has 5 equal beds. 2 have flowers. How many fifths have no flowers?
A pie has 3 equal pieces. 1 is left. How many thirds were eaten?
A bar has 6 equal pieces. 4 are shaded. How many sixths are not shaded?
Which is larger: 3/8 or 5/8?
questions.solution: Same-sized pieces (eighths): 5 of them is more than 3.

misconceptions.says: Both are eighths, the same size of piece. 5 pieces are more than 3.

questions.prompt: Which is smallest: 4/9, 7/9 or 2/9?
questions.solution: All ninths: 2 pieces is the fewest.

questions.prompt: Put in order, smallest first: 5/6, 1/6, 3/6
questions.solution: Same pieces (sixths), so order by the top: 1/6, 3/6, 5/6.
questions.hint: The pieces are the same size. Compare how many.

questions.prompt: Which is larger: 6/10 or 4/10?
Which is larger: 2/5 or 4/5?
questions.solution: Fifths: 4 of them is more than 2.

questions.prompt: □/7 is larger than 4/7 and smaller than 6/7. What number goes in the box?
questions.solution: Sevenths: more than 4 and fewer than 6 is 5.

misconceptions.says: 4/7 is equal to 4/7, not larger.
6/7 is equal to 6/7, not smaller.

questions.prompt: Which is smaller: 5/9 or 7/9?
questions.solution: Ninths: 5 of them is fewer than 7.

misconceptions.says: The pieces stay eighths. Add the tops only: 5/8.
The pieces stay tenths: 3/10.

questions.hint: The size of the pieces does not change. Count them.

misconceptions.says: Ninths plus ninths are still ninths: 7/9.

questions.prompt: Which equals 2/5 + 1/5?
questions.solution: 2 fifths + 1 fifth = 3 fifths. The bottom stays 5.

misconceptions.says: Add the tops only: the pieces are still fifths, so 3/5.
7 + 8 = 15. Multiplying means 8 groups of 7.
Close: 7 × 8 is 56.
48 is 6 × 8. 7 × 8 is one more 8: 56.
6 + 7 = 13. Multiplying means 6 groups of 7.

questions.prompt: Quick one: 7 × 7 = ?
Quick one: 7 × 5 = ?
Quick one: 7 × 3 = ?
Quick one: 7 × 2 = ?
Quick one: 7 + 7 + 7 = ?

questions.hint: 8 × 9 is one more group of 8 than 8 × 8.

questions.prompt: 6 × 8 = ? (Split 8 into 5 + 3 if it helps.)

misconceptions.says: 6 + 8 = 14; we need 8 groups of 6.

questions.prompt: 9 × 8 = ? (9 × 2 = 18; keep doubling.)
An array has 3 rows of 6 dots. How many dots?
questions.hint: Count one row, then add a row at a time.

questions.prompt: An array has 4 rows of 6 dots. How many dots?
Which equals 8 × 6?
A rectangle is 6 cm long and 4 cm wide. What is its area in square centimetres?

misconceptions.says: 20 is the perimeter (6 + 4 + 6 + 4). Area is length × width: 24.

questions.prompt: A square has sides of 5 m. What is its area in square metres?

misconceptions.says: 20 is the perimeter. Area is 5 × 5 = 25.

questions.prompt: A rectangle is 9 m by 3 m. Area in square metres?
A rectangle is 8 cm by 5 cm. Area in square centimetres?
A rectangle is 7 m by 4 m. Area in square metres?
Which rectangle has an area of 36 square centimetres?
A rectangle is 9 cm by 3 cm. Area in square centimetres?
Which point is 3 to the right of the origin and 2 down?

misconceptions.says: x comes first and goes across; y goes up or down.

questions.prompt: The point (4, 7) is how far above the x-axis?
Which point is on the y-axis?
questions.hint: Which point has no movement across?

questions.prompt: The point (−6, 2) is how far from the y-axis?
In which quadrant is (−2, −5)?
In which quadrant is (−3, 4)?
questions.solution: x negative, y positive: the second quadrant.

questions.prompt: In which quadrant is (4, −1)?
questions.solution: x positive, y negative: the fourth quadrant.

questions.prompt: The integral of 3 from x = 0 to x = 4 is the area of a rectangle. What is it?
∫ from 1 to 5 of 2 dx = ?

misconceptions.says: The width is 5 − 1 = 4, not 5: 2 × 4 = 8.

questions.prompt: ∫ from 0 to 6 of 5 dx = ?
∫ from 2 to 7 of 4 dx = ?
∫ from 0 to 3 of 9 dx = ?
Which equals ∫ from 1 to 5 of 6 dx?
∫ from 2 to 6 of 5 dx = ?
Find ∫ from 0 to 8 of 7 dx: the area under y = 7 from x = 0 to x = 8.
questions.solution: The region is a rectangle 8 wide and 7 high: 8 × 7 = 56.

misconceptions.says: 15 is 7 + 8. The area of the rectangle is 7 × 8.
The method is right: the area is 7 × 8. The multiplication fact is 56.

questions.prompt: Find ∫ from 0 to 9 of 6 dx.
How many factors does 12 have? (Count 1 and 12.)

misconceptions.says: Remember 1 and 12 themselves: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12.

questions.prompt: What is the smallest number, other than 0, that is a multiple of both 4 and 6?

misconceptions.says: 24 works, but 12 is smaller.
2 is a common factor. A multiple is in the times table: 12.

questions.prompt: How many factors does 18 have?
What is the smallest number, other than 0, that is a multiple of both 6 and 8?
How many factors does 20 have?
Which is a factor of 18?
questions.solution: 18 = 6 × 3, so 6 is a factor. 4, 5 and 7 do not divide 18.

questions.prompt: How many factors does 15 have?
Reasoning challenge: find the smallest number greater than 1 that leaves remainder 1 when divided by 2, by 3 and by 4.
questions.solution: A multiple of 12 (the smallest common multiple of 2, 3, 4) plus 1: 12 + 1 = 13.

questions.prompt: Pattern challenge: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, … What is the 8th number?
Reasoning challenge: Meena says every number ending in 1 is prime. Which number shows she is wrong?
questions.solution: 21 = 3 × 7 ends in 1 but is not prime.

questions.prompt: Solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0. Give both solutions, separated by a comma.
questions.solution: Two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to 5: 2 and 3. (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0, so x = 2 or x = 3.

misconceptions.says: (x + 2)(x + 3) gives + 5x. Here it is − 5x, so the factors are (x − 2)(x − 3): x = 2 or 3.
6 is the constant term, not a solution. Find x that makes the expression zero.

questions.prompt: x² = 49 and x is positive. What is x?

misconceptions.says: x² means x × x, not x × 2. 7 × 7 = 49.

questions.prompt: How many real solutions does x² + 1 = 0 have?
questions.solution: x² is never negative, so x² + 1 is at least 1 and is never 0: no real solutions.

misconceptions.says: A square is never negative, so x² = −1 has no real solution.

questions.prompt: Solve x² − 7x + 12 = 0.
questions.hint: Find two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7.

questions.prompt: Solve x² − x − 6 = 0.

misconceptions.says: Check the middle term: (x − 2)(x + 3) gives + x. We need − x: (x + 2)(x − 3).

questions.prompt: Solve x² + 5x + 4 = 0.
Which number is a solution of x² − 9 = 0?
A rectangle is 2 cm longer than it is wide. Its area is 15 cm². How wide is it, in cm?
questions.solution: w(w + 2) = 15, so w² + 2w − 15 = 0, (w + 5)(w − 3) = 0. A width is positive: w = 3.

questions.prompt: How many real solutions does x² = 16 have?
How many real solutions does x² + 4 = 0 have?
Solve x² − 8x + 15 = 0.
Solve x² + x − 2 = 0.
A bar is cut into 5 equal parts and 2 are shaded. What fraction is shaded?

misconceptions.says: 2/3 compares shaded with unshaded parts; a fraction compares shaded parts with all the equal parts.
The top and bottom are swapped: the bottom counts all the equal parts.
3/5 is the part that is not shaded.

questions.prompt: A ribbon is cut into 8 equal pieces. Sam uses 3 pieces for a gift. How many eighths of the ribbon are left?
□/9 is smaller than 3/9 and larger than 1/9. What number goes in the box?
questions.solution: Ninths: more than 1 and fewer than 3 is 2.

questions.prompt: Asha ate 2/6 of a cake and Ravi ate 4/6 of the same cake. Who ate more?
questions.solution: Both are sixths of the same cake: 4 pieces are more than 2.

misconceptions.says: Both are sixths of one cake, so the one with more sixths ate more.
The bottom numbers were added too; sevenths stay sevenths.

questions.prompt: A jug is 2/9 full. You pour in another 5/9 of a jug. How full is it now?

misconceptions.says: The bottom numbers were added too; ninths stay ninths.
48 is 8 × 6. 7 × 6 is one 6 less: 42.
7 and 6 were added; 7 × 6 is 7 groups of 6.

questions.prompt: Chairs are set out in 8 rows of 7. How many chairs are there?
A rectangle is 9 cm by 4 cm. What is its area in square centimetres?

misconceptions.says: 26 cm is the perimeter (the distance around); area is the space inside: 9 × 4.
The sides were added; area multiplies them.

questions.prompt: A floor is 6 m long and 5 m wide. How many tiles 1 m by 1 m cover it?
The point (−4, □) is on the x-axis. What number goes in the box?
questions.solution: Every point on the x-axis has y = 0.

questions.prompt: On a map grid you start at (1, 2) and move 3 units left. What is your new x-coordinate?

misconceptions.says: Moving left makes x smaller, not larger.
The sign was dropped: 1 − 3 is −2.

questions.prompt: ∫ from 2 to 7 of 3 dx = ?

misconceptions.says: Only the upper limit was used; the width is 7 − 2.
The whole numbers from 2 to 7 were counted; the width is 7 − 2 = 5.

questions.prompt: A tap adds water at a steady 4 litres per minute from minute 3 to minute 10. The water added is ∫ from 3 to 10 of 4 dt. How many litres is that?
questions.solution: Width 10 − 3 = 7 minutes, height 4 litres per minute: 7 × 4 = 28 litres.

questions.prompt: What is the smallest number that is a multiple of both 4 and 6?

misconceptions.says: 4 × 6 = 24 is a common multiple, but 12 is smaller.

questions.prompt: A class of 24 is split into equal teams of more than 1 and fewer than 24 pupils. How many different team sizes are possible?
questions.solution: The factors of 24 between 2 and 23: 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12. That is 6 sizes.
